sections.kicker: 01 · Why Fat Is the Real Fuel Tank

blocks.x: Glycogen is the pantry; fat is the warehouse. Of everything your body stores as usable energy, triacylglycerol accounts for about 84%, protein about 15%, and carbohydrate (glucose plus glycogen) less than 1%. Fat also carries more than twice the energy per gram — 9 kcal/g — because its carbons are highly reduced and there is no water bound to it.

The pathway that unlocks that store is β-oxidation, so named because the chemistry happens at the β-carbon (C-3) of the fatty acid. It chops long chains into two-carbon units of acetyl-CoA, which then feed the Krebs cycle and the electron transport chain.

blocks.title: Everyday scenario — the pantry and the warehouse

blocks.x: You met glycogen as the kitchen pantry: small, instant, gone in a day. Fat is the warehouse across town — enormous, slower to reach, but it is what actually carries you through a long fast, an overnight sleep, or a marathon. Nobody survives a night on pantry snacks alone; you live on the warehouse without ever noticing.
Dietary fat is not a minor contributor either: fats supply roughly 30–60% of the calories in an average diet, mostly as triacylglycerols from dairy, meats, oils and nuts.

sections.title: Structure, naming, and the ones you must eat

blocks.x: A fatty acid is an amphipathic molecule: a polar carboxyl head and a non-polar hydrocarbon tail. Over a hundred types exist, and they differ in only three ways worth remembering.

items: Chain length: very-long (>20 C), long (C12–C20), medium (C6–C12), short (C4).
Degree of unsaturation: saturated, monounsaturated or polyunsaturated.
Position of double bonds: which gives us the omega-3 and omega-6 families.

blocks.x: Reading the shorthand. C18:1 Δ9 means 18 carbons, one double bond, positioned at carbon 9 counting from the carboxyl carbon — that is oleic acid. The omega (ω) system counts from the opposite end, the tail. So linolenate is 18:3 Δ9,12,15 and also 18:3 ω3,6,9 — the same molecule, counted from the other side.

Essential fatty acids. Mammals cannot introduce double bonds beyond carbon 9. That single enzymatic limitation is why linoleate, linolenate and arachidonate must come from the diet — they are the essential fatty acids.

blocks.title: Everyday scenario — why omega-3 is on every food label

blocks.x: The omega numbering is just counting from the tail instead of the head, and it survives in advertising because omega-3s (found in salmon, mackerel, flaxseed, soybean and walnut) are ones we genuinely cannot make. When a label boasts about omega-3, it is quietly telling you it contains something your enzymes are incapable of building.

sections.title: Digestion, transport and mobilisation

blocks.x: Fat has an obvious problem: it must be digested and transported in water. The solution is emulsification followed by packaging into lipoproteins.

Free fatty acids in the duodenum trigger release of the peptide hormone PZ-CCK, which does two jobs at once: it empties the gallbladder (delivering bile salts) and releases pancreatic enzymes, including pancreatic lipase.

items: Bile salts emulsify the fat into fine droplets, hugely increasing the surface area lipases can work on. The alkaline pancreatic juice provides the right medium.
Pancreatic lipase and phospholipase A₂ release fatty acids and glycerol from triacylglycerol, working through DAG and MAG stages.
On reabsorption these are re-formed into TAG, packaged with proteins into chylomicrons and lipoproteins, and released into the blood.
At the tissues, lipoprotein lipase hydrolyses them again so fatty acids can enter adipocytes or liver cells.
Glycerol is not wasted — it is converted to DHAP and enters glycolysis.

blocks.x: Mobilising your own fat. Stored TAG is released on demand by hormone-sensitive lipase, which is activated by glucagon and epinephrine acting on a 7-transmembrane receptor and a G-protein/cAMP cascade.

blocks.title: Everyday scenario — washing up greasy plates

blocks.x: Bile salts do exactly what dish soap does: break a large grease blob into tiny droplets so the water-based enzymes can attack them. Without soap the grease sits in one lump and the water slides off — which is precisely what happens to fat digestion when bile flow is blocked.

sections.title: Fatty acids must be 'switched on' before anything happens

blocks.x: A free fatty acid cannot be oxidised as it is. It must first be esterified to coenzyme A, forming fatty acyl-CoA. This happens on the outer mitochondrial membrane and ER, catalysed by acyl-CoA synthetase (thiokinase).
The reaction is ATP-dependent and runs in two steps:
CoASH + RCO₂H + ATP → RCO-S-CoA + AMP + PPi

Note carefully what that costs. ATP is split to AMP + PPi, not ADP + Pi, and the pyrophosphate is then hydrolysed to 2 Pi. That hydrolysis (ΔG°′ ≈ −33.6 kJ/mol) is what pulls the whole reaction forward, since the esterification itself is unfavourable (+31.5 kJ/mol). The overall change lands near −34.4 kJ/mol.
So activation costs the equivalent of 2 ATP — a fact you must subtract when totalling the energy yield. There are different acyl-CoA synthetases for different chain lengths.

blocks.title: Everyday scenario — paying the entry fee

blocks.x: Think of activation as buying a ticket before you can enter. It costs you two ATP up front, and you never get it back — but the ride you are buying returns over a hundred. Students routinely forget this fee when calculating yield, which is exactly why examiners ask about it.

sections.title: Getting long-chain fat into the matrix

blocks.x: Now a transport problem. Fatty acyl-CoA formed outside can pass the outer membrane easily (through large VDAC channels) but cannot cross the inner mitochondrial membrane. Long-chain fatty acids therefore need the carnitine shuttle.
Three steps, and the logic is simply swap the carrier, cross, swap it back:

items: 1 · CPT-I (carnitine palmitoyltransferase I), on the cytosolic face of the outer membrane, transfers the fatty acid from CoA onto carnitine, forming acylcarnitine.
2 · An antiporter in the inner membrane exchanges acylcarnitine (in) for free carnitine (out).
3 · CPT-II, inside the matrix, transfers the fatty acid back from carnitine onto CoA. The fatty acyl-CoA is now in the matrix, ready to be oxidised.

blocks.x: Remember this location: CPT-I is the rate-limiting, regulated step of the entire pathway — the control point we return to in section 09.

blocks.title: Everyday scenario — the ferry across a river with no bridge

blocks.x: The cargo (the fatty acid) cannot swim. Carnitine is the ferry, CPT-I loads it on the near bank, and CPT-II unloads it on the far bank — the ferry then returns empty for the next load. Control the ferry and you control the whole crossing, which is exactly what the body does.

sections.title: Four steps, repeated until the chain is gone

blocks.x: Now the core chemistry. Four reactions, always in the same order, and each turn releases one acetyl-CoA, one FADH₂ and one NADH while shortening the chain by two carbons.

blocks.cap: Each turn strips two carbons off the fatty acid, producing one FADH₂, one NADH and one acetyl-CoA. Because the chain gets shorter every turn, it is a spiral, not a cycle.

items: 1 · Dehydrogenation — acyl-CoA dehydrogenase creates a trans double bond between the α and β carbons (C2–C3), using FAD. It is this involvement of the β-carbon that names the whole pathway.
2 · Hydration — enoyl-CoA hydratase adds water across the double bond, giving L-3-hydroxyacyl-CoA.
3 · Dehydrogenation again — β-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase oxidises that alcohol to a ketone, using NAD⁺.
4 · Thiolysis — β-ketoacyl-CoA thiolase cleaves the bond, releasing acetyl-CoA and an acyl-CoA two carbons shorter, which re-enters at step 1.

blocks.x: Three chain-length-specific dehydrogenases handle step 1: LCAD (>C12), MCAD (C6–C12) and SCAD (C4–C6). MCAD deficiency is one of the commonest inborn errors of metabolism — worth knowing by name.

blocks.title: Everyday scenario — slicing a long loaf

blocks.x: Every pass of the knife takes exactly two slices off the end and hands them to the Krebs cycle, and the loaf that remains goes straight back under the knife. It is a spiral rather than a cycle because you never return to the same starting molecule — the chain is shorter every single time.

blocks.title: Clinical scenario — the child who cannot fast

blocks.x: In MCAD deficiency, medium-chain fatty acids cannot be oxidised. The child is completely well while eating normally, then a simple stomach bug and a missed meal produces hypoglycaemia and collapse, because the body cannot switch over to burning fat. It is a metabolic pathway made visible only when it is needed.

sections.title: Palmitate, from start to finish

blocks.x: Take palmitate (C16), the standard worked example. Sixteen carbons means 7 turns of the spiral and 8 acetyl-CoA — not 8 turns, because the final turn splits a four-carbon unit into two acetyl-CoAs.
Palmitoyl-CoA + 7 FAD + 7 CoA + 7 H₂O → 8 acetyl-CoA + 7 FADH₂ + 7 NADH + 7H⁺
Adding it up on the modern convention (NADH = 2.5 ATP, FADH₂ = 1.5 ATP):

items: Activation: −2 ATP (the entry fee from section 04).
7 FADH₂ from acyl-CoA dehydrogenase → 10.5 ATP.
7 NADH from β-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase → 17.5 ATP.
8 acetyl-CoA through the Krebs cycle and oxidative phosphorylation → 80 ATP.

blocks.x: That gives roughly 106 ATP on the modern figures (about 129–131 on the older 3-and-2 convention). Whichever set your examiner uses, state the convention you are using — that is what earns the mark.
Compare that with the ~36 ATP from a whole glucose molecule and the reason fat is the storage fuel becomes obvious.

sections.title: Odd-numbered, unsaturated and branched fatty acids

blocks.x: The four-step spiral assumes a neat, even-numbered, saturated chain. Real fatty acids are not always so obliging, and each complication is solved by adding an enzyme, not rebuilding the pathway.

Odd-carbon fatty acids. Uncommon — made by bacteria in ruminant stomachs, by plants, marine organisms and the human colon. Oxidation proceeds normally until the last cleavage leaves a three-carbon propionyl-CoA. Three enzymes then rescue it:

items: Propionyl-CoA carboxylase (needs biotin) → D-methylmalonyl-CoA.
Methylmalonyl-CoA epimerase → L-methylmalonyl-CoA.
Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase (needs vitamin B₁₂) → succinyl-CoA, which enters the Krebs cycle.

blocks.x: Note what that means: odd-chain fatty acids are the one part of fat that can be partly anaplerotic, and the B₁₂ requirement is a favourite exam hook.
Unsaturated fatty acids. A naturally occurring cis bond blocks formation of the required trans-Δ² intermediate. Two extra enzymes fix this:

items: Enoyl-CoA isomerase converts a cis-Δ³ bond into the usable trans-Δ² — handling odd-numbered double bonds.
2,4-dienoyl-CoA reductase (using NADPH) deals with even-numbered double bonds, reducing the 2,4-dienoyl intermediate before the isomerase finishes the job.

blocks.x: Branched-chain fatty acids. A methyl branch blocks the β-carbon entirely, so the chain is first shortened by α-oxidation in peroxisomes (as with phytanic acid → pristanic acid), after which normal β-oxidation can proceed — yielding a mixture of acetyl-CoA, propionyl-CoA and isobutyryl-CoA.

sections.title: Malonyl-CoA, CPT-I and AMPK

blocks.x: Control of fatty acid oxidation is exerted almost entirely at one place: entry into the mitochondrion, i.e. CPT-I. Everything else follows from that.
The key inhibitor is malonyl-CoA — and the elegance is that malonyl-CoA is the first intermediate of fatty acid synthesis, made from acetyl-CoA by acetyl-CoA carboxylase (ACC).

items: High malonyl-CoA (you are building fat) → CPT-I inhibited → fat cannot enter mitochondria → oxidation stops.
Low malonyl-CoA (you are not building fat) → CPT-I active → oxidation proceeds.

blocks.x: The energy sensor sitting above all this is AMP-activated kinase (AMPK), allosterically activated by AMP — which rises exactly when ATP is low. AMPK phosphorylates and inhibits ACC, malonyl-CoA falls, CPT-I is released, fat pours into the mitochondria, and acetyl-CoA feeds the Krebs cycle to restore ATP.
Hormonally, glucagon drives this (lowering malonyl-CoA and activating the shuttle) while insulin does the reverse. The rate-controlling step for ketogenesis, likewise, is CPT-I.

blocks.title: Everyday scenario — you cannot fill and drain the tank at once

blocks.x: This is the body refusing to do something absurd: build fat and burn it simultaneously, wasting ATP on a futile cycle. The signal that says 'we are storing' is the same molecule that physically locks the door to burning. One switch, two opposite outcomes — which is exactly the design you saw with glycogen.

sections.title: What the liver does when glucose runs out

blocks.x: During fasting or carbohydrate starvation, gluconeogenesis drains oxaloacetate from the liver. Without OAA, acetyl-CoA cannot enter the Krebs cycle — and acetyl-CoA is arriving in floods from β-oxidation. The liver's answer is to convert it into ketone bodies.
There are three, and only two are true fuels:

items: Acetoacetate and β-hydroxybutyrate — the two usable, water-soluble fuels.
Acetone — the spontaneous breakdown product, largely exhaled.

blocks.x: Why this matters so much. The brain consumes around 70% of the body's glucose and about 20% of its oxygen at rest — yet free fatty acids cannot cross the blood–brain barrier, and neural tissue has little capacity for fatty acid oxidation. Ketone bodies can cross. They are, in effect, the liver converting fat into a currency the brain will accept.

items: Early fasting: heart and skeletal muscle use ketones, sparing glucose for the CNS. Heart and renal cortex actually prefer acetoacetate to glucose.
Prolonged starvation: the brain itself adapts to using ketone bodies, dramatically reducing its glucose demand.

blocks.x: The clinical edge. Ketone bodies are relatively strong acids. In excess they cause ketonemia, ketonuria and ketoacidosis. In untreated type 1 diabetes the picture becomes diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA): glucose cannot get into cells, fatty acid oxidation surges, and ketone production overwhelms the tissues' ability to use them. Acidifying the blood also impairs haemoglobin's ability to bind oxygen. Acetone on the breath can even be measured by gas chromatography.

blocks.title: Everyday scenario — fruity breath and the keto diet

blocks.x: That distinctive sweet, nail-polish smell on the breath of someone in DKA — or a few days into a strict low-carbohydrate diet — is acetone being exhaled. Same biochemistry, wildly different severity: mild, regulated ketosis in a dieter; life-threatening, unregulated ketoacidosis in untreated diabetes.

One caution worth carrying: in acute hypoglycaemia (too much insulin, or alcohol), the brain is cut off from glucose abruptly, before ketone-using enzymes can be induced. Without fuel it cannot pump ions, fire signals or repair itself — producing confusion, then coma. Adaptation to ketones takes time the patient does not have.

sections.title: Key takeaways

blocks.x: The short version of a long topic.

items: Fat is the main store (~84% of stored energy, 9 kcal/g) and β-oxidation is how it is spent.
Activation costs 2 ATP (ATP → AMP + PPi) and happens outside the mitochondrion.
The carnitine shuttle (CPT-I → antiporter → CPT-II) carries long-chain fat in — and CPT-I is the control point.
Four steps per turn: dehydrogenate (FAD), hydrate, dehydrogenate (NAD⁺), thiolytic cleavage — yielding 1 acetyl-CoA + 1 FADH₂ + 1 NADH and a chain 2 carbons shorter.
Palmitate = 7 turns, 8 acetyl-CoA, ~106 ATP net on modern conventions.
Malonyl-CoA inhibits CPT-I, so synthesis and oxidation can never run at once; AMPK tips the balance toward burning.
Ketone bodies let the liver send fat-derived fuel to the brain — invaluable in fasting, dangerous in uncontrolled diabetes.

blocks.x: And the links backwards: acetyl-CoA from here enters the Krebs cycle, its NADH and FADH₂ feed the electron transport chain, and the whole pathway is switched on precisely when glycogen has run out. This topic is where all of biochemistry's energy pathways finally meet.

lines: Oxidation, Hydration, Oxidation, Thiolysis — the same four steps repeating, giving one FADH₂, one NADH and one acetyl-CoA each turn.

mnemonics.h: CPT-I is the gate, malonyl-CoA is the lock
lines: Nothing long-chain gets into the matrix without CPT-I, and malonyl-CoA from the fed state shuts it — you cannot make fat and burn it at once.
Activation costs two ATP equivalents because ATP is split to AMP and pyrophosphate, not to ADP — easy marks lost by forgetting to subtract it.
An odd-numbered chain ends in propionyl-CoA, which reaches succinyl-CoA through a vitamin B12-dependent mutase — the one place B12 meets fat metabolism.
Palmitate (C16) takes 7 cycles to give 8 acetyl-CoA — always one fewer cycle than the number of acetyl-CoA produced.
Location: mitochondrial matrix — very long chains start in peroxisomes
Fuel of choice for heart, resting muscle and the fasting liver
Fatty acid + CoA + ATP → acyl-CoA + AMP + PPi (acyl-CoA synthetase)
Costs 2 ATP equivalents, since ATP goes all the way to AMP
CPT-I on the outer membrane — the rate-limiting step
Translocase across the inner membrane, then CPT-II regenerates acyl-CoA
Malonyl-CoA inhibits CPT-I — the fed-state brake on fat burning
Oxidation (FAD) → Hydration → Oxidation (NAD+) → Thiolysis
Each turn: 1 FADH₂ + 1 NADH + 1 acetyl-CoA, chain 2 carbons shorter
7 cycles → 8 acetyl-CoA + 7 FADH₂ + 7 NADH
Net ≈ 106 ATP once the 2 spent on activation are subtracted
Odd-chain: ends in propionyl-CoA → methylmalonyl-CoA → succinyl-CoA (B12)
Unsaturated: needs an isomerase, plus a reductase for polyunsaturates
Very long chain: peroxisomal, first oxidation gives H₂O₂ not FADH₂
Fasting liver: surplus acetyl-CoA → acetoacetate, β-hydroxybutyrate, acetone
Fuel for brain and muscle; the liver itself cannot use them

items.d: Hormone-sensitive lipase, activated by glucagon and adrenaline and inhibited by insulin, releases free fatty acids that travel on albumin.
Acyl-CoA synthetase on the outer mitochondrial membrane: fatty acid + CoA + ATP → acyl-CoA + AMP + PPi. Costs two ATP equivalents.
CPT-I swaps CoA for carnitine, translocase carries acylcarnitine across, CPT-II restores acyl-CoA in the matrix. CPT-I is rate-limiting and malonyl-CoA inhibits it.
A double bond is made between the α and β carbons, reducing FAD to FADH₂. Chain-length-specific enzymes here — MCAD deficiency is the common inherited defect.
Water adds across the new double bond, putting a hydroxyl group on the β carbon.
The β-hydroxyl is oxidised to a keto group, reducing NAD+ to NADH.
A second CoA cleaves off the terminal two carbons as acetyl-CoA, leaving an acyl-CoA two carbons shorter to re-enter step 4.
